title: Percentages you will actually use
hook: A 230 V supply loses 9 V along a cable run. What percentage is that, and how many volts would 3% be?
oneBreath: A percentage is a number out of a hundred, so 15% is 15 hundredths, or 0.15, and 15% of an amount is that amount times 0.15. To say what percentage one amount is of another, divide the part by the whole and times by 100. To raise or cut by a percentage in one step, times by a multiplier: up 20% is × 1.2 and down 15% is × 0.85. A percentage change is the change divided by the original amount, times 100, so a fall comes out negative. To get back to the amount before a rise or cut, divide by the multiplier, which is why up 20% and then down 20% does not bring you back to the start.

ideas.title: What a percentage is
ideas.oneLine: 15% means 15 out of every 100, so it is 0.15 or 15/100, and 15% of an amount is that amount × 0.15.

ideas.title: What percentage is it?
ideas.oneLine: Divide the part by the whole and times by 100, so a 9 V drop on 230 V is about 3.9%.

ideas.title: Up or down by a percentage
ideas.oneLine: Raise or cut in one step with a multiplier: up 20% is × 1.2, and down 15% is × 0.85.

ideas.title: Percentage change
ideas.oneLine: A percentage change is the change divided by the original amount, times 100, so a fall comes out negative.

ideas.title: Back to the original
ideas.oneLine: To find the amount before a rise or cut, divide by the multiplier, which is why up 20% then down 20% ends at 96%.

calibration.why: 10% of £40 is £4 and 5% is half that, £2, so 15% is £6, the same as 40 × 0.15. £2.67 divides by 15 instead, and £0.60 reads 15% as 0.015.

calibration.q: A part's price goes up from £400 to £500. By what percentage has it risen?
calibration.why: The rise is £100, and you compare it with where it started: 100 ÷ 400 × 100 = 25%. 20% compares it with the new price, and 100% treats the £100 rise as the percentage.
